subject: Version Control Systems

assessmentTargets.subtopic: Git workflow areas and git add
assessmentTargets.concept: Identify the three Git areas (working directory, staging area, repository) and explain how `git add` moves changes from the working directory to the staging area.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: The next one you have is git add. So this is, if you remember in your git workflow, I told you we have three areas. Working directory, staging area and git repository. So from working directory, if you want to move your project into staging area, where you are deciding which changes have to be saved, then you have to use a command called as git add.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Explanation of three areas and purpose of git add.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to label each area and describe the effect of `git add .`.

assessmentTargets.concept: Demonstrate how to create a repository snapshot using `git commit -m "message"` and describe the role of the commit message.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: Then you have to go for the next one, which is called as git commit. Git commit will save the changes of your particular file into the repository... you have to use a command git commit. And you have to give a message.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Description of git commit and its message requirement.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Provide a file change and ask the learner to commit it with an appropriate message.

assessmentTargets.concept: Analyze the output of `git diff` to identify differences between the current working state and the previous commit.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: The next one is git diff... If you want to see the difference between your previous commit and the current commit... then you have to use a command which is called as git diff. It will compare the changes of your current file with the previous version.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Present a modified file and ask the learner to interpret the diff output.

assessmentTargets.subtopic: Undoing changes: git reset & git restore
assessmentTargets.concept: Evaluate when to use `git reset` versus `git restore` to revert staged or working‑directory changes.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: I will simply write git reset. When you type git reset all the changes will be reverted back... I will simply type git restore . When I do that ... the new line is also deleted.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Demonstration of git reset and git restore for undoing changes.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Give a scenario with staged changes and ask the learner to choose and justify the appropriate undo command.

assessmentTargets.concept: Use `git help <command>` to retrieve syntax, options, and examples for any Git command.
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: Now say suppose you forgot how to use a particular command in git. Then simply write git help that command name. It will give you the manual page... it will give you the complete details of what is that command, how to use it, what is its syntax, it will give you some examples, what are the various options of that particular command.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to retrieve help for `git add` and list two options shown.

reserveTargets.concept: Explain how `git init` converts a normal folder into a local Git repository.
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: You have to type git init. This particular folder which is called as sample example is converted into a git repository.
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: Demonstration of git init creating a repository.
reserveTargets.instruction: Prompt the learner to identify the hidden .git directory after initialization.

reserveTargets.concept: Interpret the color‑coded output of `git status` to determine file states (untracked, staged, clean).
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: Now to know whatever changes you have made in this particular project you have to type git status. It is telling there is one file called a.ext in which you did not save anything... after git add . the file turns green indicating it is staged.
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: Description of git status output before and after staging.
reserveTargets.instruction: Present a screenshot of `git status` and ask the learner to label each file state.
